title: India's Corporate Borrowers Are Racing to Lock In Lower Rates. The RBI's Dollar Blitz Just Opened a Window.
excerpt: Companies have launched more than $3 billion in bond sales this week after the central bank's forex measures slashed borrowing costs by 40 basis points. For NRI fixed-income investors, the calculus is shifting.
body:
When the Reserve Bank of India opened its dollar spigot last Friday, the corporate treasury desks in Mumbai did not wait for Monday's newspapers. They moved.

Indian companies are raising more than 310 billion rupees — approximately $3.24 billion — through bond issuances of up to five years this week, according to four merchant bankers who spoke to Reuters. The supply equals roughly one-third of what was raised across all of April and May combined.

The catalyst is a cluster of measures the RBI announced on June 6 to draw dollars into the country: subsidised forex swap facilities for banks' overseas borrowings, incentives for state-run companies to raise funds abroad, and enhanced limits on foreign-currency non-resident (FCNR) deposits. The immediate effect has been a sharp compression in corporate borrowing costs — down 40 to 45 basis points across AAA-rated bonds of up to five years, according to LSEG benchmark data.

Corporate bond yields had touched their highest levels in seven years in May, battered by the Iran war's energy shock, persistent foreign portfolio investor outflows, and the RBI's earlier rate pause.

Now the floor has dropped. And the scramble is on.

## Who Is Borrowing

Non-banking financial companies are leading the charge. State-run REC locked in three-year funds at a coupon of 7.34 per cent earlier this week — significantly below prevailing secondary-market rates. NABARD, which had cancelled a similar issue in May when rates threatened to touch 8 per cent, returned successfully at the same 7.34 per cent.

The pipeline behind them is substantial. Bajaj Finance has lined up issuances worth 85 billion rupees. Muthoot Finance is raising 27.5 billion rupees. Bajaj Housing Finance and L&T Finance have planned 20 billion and 15 billion rupees, respectively.

"A rise in overseas borrowings could reduce the need for local debt supply, leading to a rally in bonds below five years," said Ajay Marwaha, head of fixed-income markets at Nuvama.

The logic is circular but functional: RBI subsidises foreign borrowing, which reduces domestic debt supply, which pushes yields lower, which draws in more issuers while the window is open.

## The Macro Backdrop Is Still Fragile

The bond rush should not be mistaken for calm. India's equity benchmarks remain under severe pressure. The Nifty 50 has fallen 7.8 per cent since the Iran war began in late February, with about $30 billion in foreign outflows — the largest exit in the country's history. Foreign portfolio investors sold another $223 million of Indian shares on Wednesday alone, marking nine consecutive sessions of selling.

The Iran war, now in its fourth month, continues to roil energy markets. Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed this week after fresh US strikes, and President Trump vowed more attacks if no peace deal is secured. Brent crude has hovered near $93 per barrel, keeping India's current-account deficit elevated and the rupee under pressure.

But the RBI's measures are not designed to fix any of that. They are designed to buy time — to stabilise the rupee, compress credit spreads, and signal to the market that the central bank has tools left.

For now, it is working. Investor appetite for the new bonds remains strong, merchant bankers say, on expectations of further gains.

## What NRI Fixed-Income Investors Should Know

The implications cut both ways for non-resident investors.

On deposits, the picture is still favourable. Indian banks continue to offer NRIs up to 7 per cent on FCNR dollar deposits — rates backstopped by the RBI's new hedging subsidy. That window remains open until September, and for NRIs sitting on dollar savings, it is one of the best risk-adjusted returns available in a high-rate global environment.

On Indian corporate bonds, the picture is more nuanced. The 40-basis-point compression means yields are lower than they were a month ago. NRIs investing through portfolio routes may find the entry less attractive than it was in May, though absolute yields on AAA-rated paper — still above 7 per cent for three-year tenors — remain elevated by historical standards.

The strategic question is duration. If the RBI's measures succeed in pulling dollars into India and stabilising the rupee, bond prices will rise further, rewarding those who locked in now. If the Iran war escalates and oil pushes past $100, even the RBI's subsidies may prove insufficient, and yields could reverse course.

"Crude oil remains the joker in the pack as the impact of the Iran war plays out," said Vikas Satija, managing director and CEO at Shriram Wealth.

## The Window May Not Stay Open

Bond markets operate on urgency. The companies rushing to raise capital this week understand something fundamental: the RBI's measures created a temporary dislocation between policy rates and market rates. That gap is an opportunity, not a new equilibrium.

If geopolitical conditions deteriorate, if oil breaches $100 sustainably, or if the Fed signals higher-for-longer rates in response to May's CPI overshoot, the window closes.

India's corporate sector is not waiting to find out.
